variants.title: Write the contract in order
variants.context: A useful contract joins the client intent, the resource, request semantics, and the response promise. Write those down in order before a handler exists.
variants.prompt: A team is adding “cancel an order”. Put the contract steps in order.

items.text: Name the client intent: record a cancellation.
Choose the resource: a cancellation record under the order.
Set request semantics: method, validation, and whether repeating is safe.
Publish the response promise: success and error shapes, fields that may be added, deprecation timing.

variants.explanation: Intent → resource → request semantics → response promise. Starting from a table or controller name produces contracts that leak implementation.

variants.title: Write the contract in order
variants.context: A useful contract joins the client intent, the resource, request semantics, and the response promise. Write those down in order before a handler exists.
variants.prompt: A new “list orders” endpoint is planned. Put the steps in order.

items.text: State the outcome the client wants: see their orders.
Expose the collection resource with a stable path.
Define filters, page controls, authentication, and that the read is safe to repeat.
Document the envelope, status codes, and compatibility promise.

variants.hint: A URL is not the design by itself.
variants.explanation: The same four steps apply to reads. Filters and page controls describe a read of the collection and never mutate it.

variants.title: Write the contract in order
variants.context: A useful contract joins the client intent, the resource, request semantics, and the response promise. Write those down in order before a handler exists.
variants.prompt: A payment capture is being exposed. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Name the intent: capture an authorized payment once.
Model the capture as a resource with its own lifecycle.
Set semantics: POST with an idempotency key and documented retry behavior.
Publish success, conflict, and failure shapes and the sunset policy.

variants.hint: An irreversible action deserves its own resource and lifecycle.
variants.explanation: Modeling the capture as a resource keeps its audit trail visible and makes the retry contract explicit.

variants.title: Pick the status
variants.context: Use status codes for the broad outcome and the body for details: 400/422 for a readable request that breaks the contract, 401/403 for identity and permission, 404 for absent or undiscoverable, 409/429 for state conflict or rate limit, 5xx for service failure.
variants.prompt: A request is well-formed JSON, but quantity is negative and the currency code is unknown. Which response?
options: 400 or 422 with field-level errors the client can fix.
optionFeedback: The request is readable but breaks the contract; tell the client which fields to fix.
Permission is not the problem; the caller is allowed, the data is wrong.
The service did not fail; the request did.
variants.hint: Who can fix this: the caller or the service?
variants.explanation: Validation failures belong to the caller. Return a 4xx with field-level detail, never a 5xx.

variants.title: Pick the status
variants.context: Use status codes for the broad outcome and the body for details: 400/422 for a readable request that breaks the contract, 401/403 for identity and permission, 404 for absent or undiscoverable, 409/429 for state conflict or rate limit, 5xx for service failure.
variants.prompt: An authenticated user tries to read another tenant’s order. Which response?
options: 403 Forbidden, or 404 if the policy is that the resource must be undiscoverable.
optionFeedback: Identity is valid; permission is missing. Some APIs return 404 to avoid revealing existence; document the choice.
The request is fine; the caller lacks permission.
An empty 200 hides a policy decision and confuses clients.
variants.hint: Is the problem the request shape, or who is asking?
variants.explanation: 401 and 403 describe identity and permission. Do not use them as a substitute for validation, and decide the privacy policy for 404.

variants.title: Pick the status
variants.context: Use status codes for the broad outcome and the body for details: 400/422 for a readable request that breaks the contract, 401/403 for identity and permission, 404 for absent or undiscoverable, 409/429 for state conflict or rate limit, 5xx for service failure.
variants.prompt: A cancellation arrives for an order that has already shipped. Which response?
options: 409 Conflict with a resolution rule in the body.
optionFeedback: A known state conflict prevents progress; tell the client how to resolve it.
The order exists; it is in the wrong state.
Accepting work that cannot happen misleads the client.
variants.hint: The resource exists but is in a state that blocks the change.
variants.explanation: 409 signals a state conflict. Include what the client can do next.

variants.title: Choose the continuation
variants.context: Pagination is a continuation contract. Offset suits small static lists; cursors suit changing ordered collections and must be opaque; always cap the page size and return next_cursor only when another page exists.
variants.prompt: A feed of orders changes while a client pages through it, and offset paging shows duplicates. What is the fix?
options: Cursor pagination with a deterministic sort and tie-breaker.
optionFeedback: A cursor carries the last observed position, so inserts before it do not shift the window.
Bigger offsets still shift when rows are inserted before them.
variants.hint: What must the next request carry to resume exactly where it stopped?
variants.explanation: Cursors resume after a position. Offsets count rows, which move when the collection changes.

variants.title: Choose the continuation
variants.context: Pagination is a continuation contract. Offset suits small static lists; cursors suit changing ordered collections and must be opaque; always cap the page size and return next_cursor only when another page exists.
variants.prompt: An internal admin list has 40 mostly static rows. Which pagination is reasonable?
optionFeedback: Small, static lists are what offset paging works well for.
A snapshot job is for complete reconcilable datasets, not a small list.
Always set a maximum page size, even for small lists.
variants.hint: Match the mechanism to how the collection changes.
variants.explanation: Offset paging is fine when the list is small and stable. Its failure mode appears with inserts and deep offsets.

variants.title: Choose the continuation
variants.context: Pagination is a continuation contract. Offset suits small static lists; cursors suit changing ordered collections and must be opaque; always cap the page size and return next_cursor only when another page exists.
variants.prompt: A client decodes the cursor, edits the position inside, and sends it back. What does the contract say?
options: The cursor is an opaque token; clients must not parse or manufacture it.
Clients may edit cursors as long as the sort is deterministic.
Cursors are public and documented for editing.
optionFeedback: Opaque cursors let the server change encoding and reject invalid tokens.
Deterministic sort is a server obligation; it does not license clients to forge positions.
variants.hint: Who owns the meaning of the cursor?
variants.explanation: Treat the cursor as a token. Document cursor expiry and invalidation responses instead.

variants.title: Make the retry safe
variants.context: Idempotency means repeated delivery of one logical operation has the same visible result as delivering it once. The client generates a key; the service stores key, caller, request fingerprint, state, and response with the write.
variants.prompt: A create-order request may time out and be retried. Put the idempotency protocol in order.

items.text: The client generates a high-entropy Idempotency-Key for one logical operation.
The service stores the key, caller, request fingerprint, processing state, and response with the authoritative write.
A repeat with the same key and matching request returns the saved result.
The service expires records only after the documented retry window.

variants.hint: The key must exist before the first attempt is sent.
variants.explanation: Generate → store with the write → replay the saved result → expire after the retry window. A repeat with different parameters is a conflict, not a second order.

variants.title: Make the retry safe
variants.context: Idempotency means repeated delivery of one logical operation has the same visible result as delivering it once. The client generates a key; the service stores key, caller, request fingerprint, state, and response with the write.
variants.prompt: A payment capture must never happen twice. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Client creates one key for this capture and reuses it only for retries.
Service persists key, fingerprint, and state together with the capture.
Repeated key with the same request returns the first response; a different request is rejected as a conflict.
Records expire after the retry window; replay and conflict rates are measured.

variants.hint: Storing the key separately from the write reopens the race.
variants.explanation: The key and the write must commit together. Otherwise a crash between them lets a retry charge again.

variants.title: Make the retry safe
variants.context: Idempotency means repeated delivery of one logical operation has the same visible result as delivering it once. The client generates a key; the service stores key, caller, request fingerprint, state, and response with the write.
variants.prompt: A downstream email provider is involved. Put the steps in order, including the downstream handoff.

items.text: Client generates the Idempotency-Key.
Service stores the key and result with the write and carries a stable operation ID downstream.
A retry with the same key returns the saved result without a second downstream call.
An outbox or reconciliation handles a side effect that completes after the client timed out.

variants.hint: Idempotency does not make side effects disappear on its own.
variants.explanation: Carry a stable operation identifier downstream and reconcile. Document what happens when a side effect finishes after the original timeout.

variants.title: Bound the page
variants.context: Pagination is a continuation contract. Offset suits small static lists; cursors suit changing ordered collections and must be opaque; always cap the page size and return next_cursor only when another page exists.
variants.prompt: The maximum page size is 100. A client requests limit=250. What effective limit does the response report?
variants.hint: The server caps the page size even when asked for more.
variants.explanation: Return the effective limit, 100, so the client knows what it actually received.

mistakes.feedback: The maximum applies regardless of the request.
The request is valid; it is capped, not rejected.

variants.title: Bound the page
variants.context: Pagination is a continuation contract. Offset suits small static lists; cursors suit changing ordered collections and must be opaque; always cap the page size and return next_cursor only when another page exists.
variants.prompt: A collection has 1,230 records and the page size is 100. How many pages does a full read take?
variants.explanation: 1,230 ÷ 100 = 12.3, so 13 pages. The last page has 30 records and no next_cursor.

mistakes.feedback: The last 30 records need a thirteenth page.
Pages are whole responses; round up.

variants.title: Bound the page
variants.context: Pagination is a continuation contract. Offset suits small static lists; cursors suit changing ordered collections and must be opaque; always cap the page size and return next_cursor only when another page exists.
variants.prompt: A collection has exactly 1,000 records and the page size is 100. How many responses include a next_cursor?
variants.hint: next_cursor appears only when another page exists.
variants.explanation: Ten pages in total; the tenth is the last, so nine responses carry a cursor.

mistakes.feedback: The final page has no next page, so no cursor.
